Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.role: Red Army artillery officer, then eight years in the Gulag
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.why: The Gulag Archipelago got him deported from the USSR in 1974. He insisted the division between good and evil is not between camps or classes but inside each person.

Alexis de Tocqueville.role: French aristocrat, magistrate, and later foreign minister
Alexis de Tocqueville.why: Toured the United States in 1831 nominally to study prisons. Democracy in America is still the best outside account of how local self-government forms citizens.

Augustine.role: Bishop of Hippo in Roman North Africa
Augustine.why: Wrote The City of God after Rome was sacked in 410, to answer the charge that Christianity had made the empire weak. It is the founding text of Christian political thought and the reason 'two cities' language exists at all.

Blaise Pascal.role: Mathematician, inventor of the mechanical calculator, Jansenist
Blaise Pascal.why: The Pensées are notes for an unfinished defence of Christianity. His writing on kings, diversion, and human greatness-in-wretchedness is the sharpest short account of why power does not satisfy.

C. S. Lewis.role: Oxford and Cambridge medievalist; served in the trenches in 1917
C. S. Lewis.why: His essays on punishment and power are unusually alert to how much damage is done by people who are certain they are helping.

Edmund Burke.role: Irish-born MP in the British Parliament for nearly thirty years
Edmund Burke.why: Prosecuted Warren Hastings over the conduct of the East India Company and defended the American colonists, then opposed the French Revolution. The founder of modern conservative political thought.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.role: Russian novelist; sentenced to death, reprieved at the scaffold, then four years in a Siberian prison camp
Fyodor Dostoevsky.why: No one has written better on what a man tells himself in order to do something monstrous, or on freedom as a burden people would rather hand to an authority.

G. K. Chesterton.role: English journalist, critic, and Catholic apologist
G. K. Chesterton.why: Argued in paradoxes because he thought the truth was shaped like one. Orthodoxy contains the best short account of why courage and humility are not opposites.

Gregory the Great.role: Pope, and a Roman prefect's son who ran the city's grain supply
Gregory the Great.why: The Book of Pastoral Rule was written to explain why he did not want the papacy. It became the standard medieval manual on the duties of anyone holding office over others.

Hannah Arendt.role: German-Jewish political theorist; fled Germany in 1933 and France in 1941
Hannah Arendt.why: Reported on the Eichmann trial for The New Yorker and concluded that the worst crimes are often committed by unremarkable people who have stopped thinking.

Hugo Grotius.role: Dutch jurist; wrote much of his major work in prison and exile
Hugo Grotius.why: The Rights of War and Peace founded modern international law, including the idea that there are things you may not do to an enemy even when you are winning.

John Chrysostom.why: Preached against the wealth and flattery of the imperial court and was exiled twice for it, dying on a forced march. On the Priesthood is his argument for why he tried to avoid ordination.

John Milton.role: Poet, and Secretary for Foreign Tongues to Cromwell's Council of State
John Milton.why: He defended regicide in print and went blind in government service. Paradise Lost gives the case for rebellion its most persuasive possible voice, which is part of its argument.

John Stuart Mill.role: English philosopher, East India Company administrator, MP
John Stuart Mill.why: Educated brutally by his father to carry on Bentham's utilitarianism, which he then substantially revised. On Liberty is the strongest defence ever written of the dissenting minority of one.

Leo Tolstoy.role: Russian novelist and, later, radical Christian anarchist
Leo Tolstoy.why: Fought at Sevastopol, then spent his last decades arguing that the Sermon on the Mount forbids force outright. His non-resistance writing directly shaped Gandhi and, through him, King.

Marcus Aurelius.role: Roman emperor for nineteen years, most of them at war
Marcus Aurelius.why: The Meditations were private notes, never meant for publication — a working ruler talking himself into restraint, written in camp on the Danube frontier.

Niccolò Machiavelli.why: The Prince is the most influential book ever written about political power detached from virtue. He is here as a genuine opponent, not a footnote — the case these passages have to answer.

Ralph Waldo Emerson.role: American essayist and former Unitarian minister
Ralph Waldo Emerson.why: Resigned his pulpit over conscience in 1832. Self-Reliance is the classic American argument for the individual against the pressure of the crowd.

Shūsaku Endō.why: Silence follows a Portuguese missionary in seventeenth-century Japan pressed to renounce his faith to stop the torture of others. It is the great novel of moral failure and what God says in it.

Simone Weil.role: French philosopher; factory worker by choice, then Republican volunteer in Spain
Simone Weil.why: Died at thirty-four in England, having restricted her food to the ration of occupied France. Wrote the essential modern essay on what force does to the person who uses it.

Søren Kierkegaard.role: Danish philosopher who published much of his work pseudonymously
Søren Kierkegaard.why: Attacked the comfortable state Christianity of his own country. Fear and Trembling is about what it costs when a command comes to one person and cannot be justified to anyone else.

Thomas Aquinas.role: Dominican friar and theologian at Paris and Naples
Thomas Aquinas.why: His treatment of law in the Summa is where the West gets the argument that an unjust law is not properly a law at all — the seed of every later appeal to a higher standard than statute.

Thomas More.role: Lord Chancellor of England under Henry VIII; executed for refusing the oath
Thomas More.why: Utopia opens with a long argument about whether a person of conscience should serve a king he cannot fully obey. More eventually answered it with his life.

William Shakespeare.why: The tragedies are the most exact study in the language of how a man reasons himself into a murder and then discovers that the killing has not finished.
